prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Courier Delivery Commitments by Destination (language en).
Grid: 3 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Destination" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Delivery" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Destination" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 161px
  col 2: header "Delivery › Window" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 71px
  col 3: header "Delivery › Conditions" · longest unbreakable word 104px · one-line width 1714px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 514px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 513px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 514px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Communicate delivery time commitments and their qualifying conditions for each destination.","reading":"Readers locate a destination, scan across to its delivery window, and read the conditions; they may also compare windows down the column. Long conditions will set much of the row height, leaving room for destination names to wrap within the same rows.","groups":["Window and Conditions belong under Delivery: the first gives the promised time range and the second qualifies it.","Destination identifies each row and anchors the comparison."],"keep_intact":["Delivery window values such as 2–3 days","Individual words and identifiers, including place names and time expressions"],"may_wrap":["Multiword destination names at word spaces","Conditions prose at natural word boundaries"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[182,92,239],"idea":"Keep destination names and delivery windows on one line, giving the remaining space to conditions."},{"name":"B","widths":[113,92,308],"idea":"Give conditions the largest possible share while allowing multiword destinations to wrap and keeping delivery windows intact."},{"name":"C","widths":[145,125,243],"idea":"Give the two delivery columns more balanced breathing room while allowing longer destination names to wrap into height likely already needed by conditions."}]}
